assessment.nobel_worthiness: The firm-heterogeneity framework changed how trade is modelled and measured. It introduced selection into exporting, productivity reallocation and a new channel for the gains from trade. It reshaped both theory and empirical work, and it builds on the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, extended it to exports versus FDI and to trade-flow estimation. Redding is an important contributor but is the more junior and more quantitative extension, so he is left out of a two-person core.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across theory, structural estimation and firm-level data. The framework is standard in graduate teaching and in policy models.
uncertainties: Heterogeneous-firm ideas also have precursors (Bernard-Jensen empirics, Hopenhayn-style selection), so credit could be argued more broadly.
Helpman's contributions also span other trade work (B013), which may complicate how the Committee frames the discovery.
My assessment relies on general knowledge, without independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model (1982) is a foundational result. It gives a unique subgame-perfect outcome and underpins strategic bargaining models across labour, trade, finance and political economy. The market-bargaining extension adds a bridge from bilateral bargaining to search and decentralised markets.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is clearly the principal originator. Wolinsky is a natural co-recipient for the bargaining-in-markets work with Rubinstein and Gale. Binmore's contributions (the Nash programme, the British Telecom-era applications, experimental links) are real but secondary to the core model.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use, and the result is canonical in textbooks. It is very mature, and the main risk is that recognition has been delayed relative to its influence.
uncertainties: The Committee may prefer to credit game theory through other themes, since recent prizes have favoured mechanism design and auctions.
Whether to include Binmore or restrict the award to Rubinstein alone is open.
Prior Nobel recognition of Nash, Harsanyi, Selten, Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson may be seen as already covering much of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Credit Cycles (1997) showed how collateral constraints propagate and amplify shocks, with durable assets serving as both collateral and productive inputs. It supplies the microfoundation behind modern macro-finance and financial-crisis models. It complements the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises without being redundant with it.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the core pair, given one seminal paper and a follow-up on liquidity. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and for empirical and quantitative work, but credit for that line partly overlaps with Bernanke's 2022 prize. Gertler also appears in B029.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of influence, reinforced by the 2008 crisis and subsequent macroprudential policy work.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee sees enough separation from the 2022 prize.
How to weigh Gertler's multiple appearances across macro candidates.
Some models are stylised, with mixed direct empirical validation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income series built from tax records transformed the empirical study of inequality and brought distributional questions back into mainstream macro and public economics. The measurement agenda has influenced policy debate and subsequent research on taxation and wealth.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the founders of the top-income series and the core of the measurement programme. Zucman's wealth and offshore-wealth work is important and more recent. The theoretical and policy interpretations by Piketty are more contested than the data contribution.
assessment.maturity: The income-series work dates to the early 2000s and is widely replicated. The wealth-distribution and offshore-wealth findings, and the broader policy claims, are more recent and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over the treatment of wealth and taxes, and over the r>g interpretation.
Whether the Committee prefers to recognise the measurement contribution separately from the contested theoretical claims.
Considerable public and political salience may complicate a purely scientific judgment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and the Taylor rule, underlies how central banks analyse and conduct monetary policy. Its practical and scientific influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely spread across at least eight names. Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the unified, welfare-based framework) are the clearest conceptual originators. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler are major contributors to estimation and implementation. The three-person limit forces difficult attribution choices.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use in policy institutions. The post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes have tested the framework but strengthened its centrality.
uncertainties: The attribution problem is severe, since several omitted contributors have strong claims.
The 2022 prize and earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Prescott-Kydland, Sargent-Sims, Phelps) cover adjacent ground.
The framework's performance in recent inflation episodes remains debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Present bias, quasi-hyperbolic discounting and reference dependence have given behavioural economics formal, portable models used in savings, health and consumer-finance research. They also support design of defaults and commitment devices in policy.
assessment.attribution: Laibson's quasi-hyperbolic and consumption-savings work and Rabin's contributions (present bias with O'Donoghue, and fairness and reference-dependent theory) are the most formal and influential. Loewenstein, O'Donoghue and Koszegi are strong contributors, but the three-person limit excludes some. The discovery is a cluster of ideas rather than a single result.
assessment.maturity: About thirty years of theory with substantial field and experimental evidence. Behavioural recognition (Kahneman 2002, Thaler 2017) is established, so the question is whether this theory cluster adds distinct value.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Kahneman and Thaler prizes.
Replication and external-validity debates for some behavioural findings.
Attribution is diffuse across psychologists and economists.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linking population tax records to measure intergenerational mobility across places and groups changed the empirical study of opportunity and produced credible evidence on neighbourhood effects. It is a major methodological and substantive advance in public and labour economics. I note that my own research includes social mobility, which is a disclosed interest rather than a reason for or against.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure of the mobility atlas and related research programme. Hendren is key to the place-effects and exposure-effects work. Friedman and Katz contribute significantly, and the work is largely collaborative, so the three-person limit makes attribution difficult.
assessment.maturity: The main results date from about 2014 onwards. Impact is large, but the long-run replication and policy-implementation record is still short compared with older candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is better seen as measurement with data access or as new theory.
Some neighbourhood and causal-effect estimates are still being tested.
Maturity is lower than that of the higher-ranked candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models integrate household heterogeneity and liquidity constraints into monetary and fiscal transmission analysis. They change conclusions about monetary-policy channels and the role of marginal propensities to consume. They are now used at central banks and in academic macro. I disclose that heterogeneous-agent macro is adjacent to my own field and to colleagues' work.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante are the clearest authors of the HANK framework (AER 2018) and the associated analysis of the monetary transmission mechanism. The tradition draws on earlier heterogeneous-agent work (Aiyagari, Huggett, Krusell-Smith) that is not on this ballot line.
assessment.maturity: Early. The framework has existed in its current form for only about eight years, so long-run empirical confirmation and independence from precursors are still unfolding.
uncertainties: Timing: the contribution may be better recognised later.
Possible need to credit the earlier incomplete-markets literature.
Competing claims from the broader heterogeneous-agent community.
